reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Onychogryphosis is a grossly thickened, opaque, curved nail that grows into a ram's-horn or oyster-shell shape, most often affecting the great toenail
It is largely a disorder of the elderly, driven by neglect, poor mobility, ill-fitting footwear, and repeated minor trauma
The nail typically deviates to one side and shows transverse ridges reflecting irregular, uneven growth
Peripheral vascular disease and any condition limiting a person's ability to reach and cut their nails predispose to it
It is often mistaken for fungal disease, but the deformity is primarily one of shape and bulk rather than infection, although secondary onychomycosis may coexist
Conservative management involves regular chiropody, mechanical thinning and reduction of the plate, and attention to footwear
Definitive treatment for a recurrent painful nail is surgical avulsion with matrix ablation to prevent regrowth
reference.pathophysiology: Onychogryphosis develops when the nail matrix produces plate at an uneven rate across its width, so that one side grows faster than the other and the nail progressively curves and twists as it thickens. Chronic low-grade trauma, pressure from footwear, impaired peripheral circulation, and simple failure to trim the nail all contribute to the disordered growth, and the accumulating layers become hard, opaque, and heaped up. The condition is self-perpetuating because the deformed plate can no longer be cut or worn down normally, allowing the characteristic hypertrophic, hooked shape to develop over months to years.
additionalDifferentials: Pachyonychia congenita and other hereditary thickening disorders
Psoriatic nail with marked subungual hyperkeratosis
Chronic pressure changes from ill-fitting footwear
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of mobility, self-care ability, and footwear
Peripheral vascular examination including pulses in elderly patients
Nail clipping for mycology to identify coexisting fungal infection
Assessment of diabetic and neuropathic status where relevant
Radiograph if an underlying bony abnormality or exostosis is suspected
Onychoscopy to help distinguish deformity from primary infection
redFlags: Underlying peripheral arterial disease or diabetes raising the risk of ulceration and infection
A painful, discharging, or ulcerated nail suggesting secondary infection or pressure necrosis
Sudden change in a long-standing deformed nail that could hide a tumour
Signs of ischaemia in the affected digit requiring vascular assessment
reference.prognosis: Onychogryphosis is a chronic, recurrent condition that responds to regular mechanical care but tends to return unless the matrix is ablated, and prognosis is closely tied to the patient's mobility, circulation, and ongoing foot care.
pitfalls: Labelling the deformity as purely fungal and relying on antifungals alone
Neglecting the vascular and diabetic status before considering nail surgery
Underestimating the role of poor self-care and footwear in recurrence
Overlooking a subungual tumour hidden beneath the hypertrophic plate
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
